what_it_does: Modern chips contain large rectangular memory blocks called macros (think: pre-built SRAM tiles or IP blocks), and deciding where to place them on the chip floorplan — a step called macro placement — has a huge impact on how fast wires can be routed between them. Getting it wrong wastes area and slows the chip. MacroDiff frames this as a generative modeling problem: instead of having an optimizer search for good (x, y) coordinates directly, it trains a diffusion model (the same class of model used in AI image generators) to learn a distribution over good layouts. The key insight is to represent each macro's position not by raw coordinates but by the lengths of wires connecting it to neighbors; wire-length representations naturally encode connectivity, are invariant to rotation and translation, and make it easier for the model to respect circuit topology. The model then generates candidate placements by running the reverse diffusion process, converting noise into a valid layout.
